x.name: Modal
x.bio: Building blocks for production AI

tweets.text:
Estimate Sandbox costs from average usage, not peak.

The full post has a calculator that shows what that might look like for your workload.

Read the full post: https://t.co/uRCSq9I7L9

Active-resource pricing bills each second, with your request as the floor (0.125 cores and 128 MiB by default, and most workloads never need to change it). Above it, a Sandbox uses spare room our scheduler leaves on its machine.

Unrelated workloads rarely peak together, so many Sandboxes can share that room, the way a power grid never has to supply every home’s peak at once.

A typical sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. At Modal, we see that pattern for coding agents, RL rollouts, and evals. Reserve for the peak, and most of what you pay for sits idle.

Modal Sandboxes burst instead, and you pay for what they use.

It’s a bad idea to pick a public fight with someone better liked than you

Sure some people resent the privileged, but absolutely no one likes a scold https://t.co/mIz4MxUBvT

Open letters and petitions can often be counterproductive

The board needs to seem like they know what they’re doing. They’re already accused of rushing the decision to force a resignation

If they’re seen as bowing to public pressure (again?) before any facts have changed, esp with the risk of bad information still to drop, it looks them look totally incompetent

A lot of people are petitioning the Nvidia board to bring back Jensen, but the first step in a negotiation is to understand the other side’s incentives and what they have to lose

Beyond the obvious duty to the company, the board’s incentives include:

1) protecting stock price:
Some of the directors have millions of tens of millions of NVDA shares. They are billionaires thanks to NVDA. If you own 28M shares, a 1% drop in stock price drops your personal wealth by like $45M

2) not getting sued:
Nvidia actually does have some d&o insurance, contrary to rumors, but being sued still isn’t a good time. The “Board has no reason to believe secrets were compromised” statement was partly CYA. If they re-hire Jensen now and more shoes drop, they would (and prob should) get sued for breach of duty

3) keeping their seat:
A corporate board membership is a superb way for retirees to make good income and have a prestigious affiliation without working too hard. When execs and investors retire, they start looking for boards to sit on, no matter the industry or the mission. Well individual board members get voted on (you can look at any 8-K for voting results), and if you’re there for a quiet retirement it’s pretty unappealing to stick your neck out

Of note: in the last election, Jensen was the board member with the highest vote at 99%, and new board chair Harvey Jones had the second lowest at 91%. Jones has been on the board since Nvidia was founded and his low vote count might even be due to perceived lack of independence from Jensen. Information to consider

x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
"Interpretable Weight-Space Programming Builds Transparent Transformers and Brain Encoding Models"

This Microsoft paper also explores whether LLMs can directly write those weights to build working models from scratch.

But instead of just maximizing accuracy, they introduce Interpretable Weight-Space Programming (iWSP), which requires LLM agents to design understandable mathematical operations, test their performance, and refine the model without backpropagation.

Using Claude Opus 5.5, iWSP builds small Transformers achieving 100% accuracy across 13 algorithmic tasks, with a median of just 166 parameters. 

It also discovers interpretable features that outperform 7 existing interpretable baselines at predicting visual-cortex activity.

https://t.co/AX5Kb7ikbG

Check out this blog on why you should write research blogs

Blogs allow you to easily share interesting research takes, publish what didn't work, and checkpoint progress without waiting on noisy review

You can now publish blogs on alphaXiv directly! https://t.co/oS59gyUIzE

"Weight-Space Reading"

Can an LLM predict how changing another model's weights will affect its behavior, without ever running that model?

This paper investigates Weight-Space Reading, where LLMs inspect the raw weights of 9B-30B parameter models using Python tools, then predict how small weight modifications will affect capabilities like math accuracy, reasoning length, and refusal behavior, without performing a single forward pass.

On subtle weight edits, Qwen3.8-27B achieves 73% balanced accuracy, compared to 57.8% when given only text descriptions of the edits.

However, the models also frequently predict changes that never happen. When 40 edits had no measurable effect on Muse-30B, the model incorrectly predicted changes for 85% of them. 

The researchers also found no conclusive evidence that LLMs are better at reading their own weights than those of other models.

https://t.co/hYLj6sOTPV

My top 5 takeaways from @nateparrott on how to get Claude to design without AI slop:

1. Give Claude context upfront.

Share screenshots, pages you like, and your past work. For an existing product, have Claude rebuild the real screens from code.

2. Research familiar UX patterns.

For hard layout problems, ask Claude to research familiar products that solve something similar and note the layouts people already know how to use.

3. Make Claude aware of its design biases.

"The model has no idea what its own biases are." In your design.md or another file, consider discouraging Claude's tells like serif text, off-white backgrounds, and card-edge bars.

4. Start with wireframes.

Have Claude create wireframes first and give it feedback to nail your core user flows before going deep on fonts and colors.

5. Ask for multiple options, then remix them.

Ask Claude for 5 options for key screens with different fonts, colors, and styles. Then pick the parts you like and ask it to remix and create 5 more options.

📌 Watch the full episode now: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX

Also available as a written post: https://t.co/jcofmkQc01

tweets.text:
The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. 

This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here.

Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before.

Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. 

Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more.

So basically tokens are only going up from here.
